messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas, a 68-year-old psychologist, presented as a man holding himself together with immense, exhausting effort. He spoke in measured tones, his clinical vocabulary a thin shield against the disarray he described. It was his wife who had finally insisted he seek help, after finding him awake for the third consecutive night, sitting rigidly in a chair facing the bedroom door. The trauma occurred two years prior, during the final, violent months of his previous marriage. His ex-wife, whose rage had been escalating for years, attacked him during a bike ride on a crowded public greenway. She had screamed at him, shoved him from his bicycle into the path of onlookers, and struck him repeatedly while he was on the ground. The public humiliation was as searing as the physical blows.

In the aftermath, the memory of the event refused to cohere. Thomas reported that he could not construct a linear story of what happened, a fact that tormented him as a professional dedicated to narrative. Instead, the trauma lived in him as a series of stark, silent photographs: the mangled front wheel of his bicycle, his ex-wife's face contorted in fury, the astonished faces in the crowd. These frozen images would flash into his mind without warning, so vivid they felt like a present-tense reality, plunging him back into a state of immediate physical danger. At other times, he would be overwhelmed by a wave of pure terror and shame, a full-body emotional echo of the event, but with no accompanying image at all. This fragmented recall served as constant, painful proof of his own failings; he had come to believe he was fundamentally inadequate, a man who couldn't even make sense of his own mind.

This conviction of his own inadequacy, coupled with the new certainty that people are not what they seem, has left him feeling perpetually unsafe. His belief that the world’s apparent order had been destroyed meant that threat could emerge from anywhere. This pervasive sense of danger dictated his movements and choices. He began watching his colleagues and students closely, scanning their faces for the subtle signs of a turn, the first hint of betrayal he was sure he had missed before. At night, this vigilance became all-consuming; he found it almost impossible to feel safe after dark and would often wake suddenly, his first instinct to check the locks and windows. The hypervigilance made his world dense with potential threats, so that even the distant glint of chrome on a bicycle handlebar across the university campus could snag his attention and cause a surge of adrenaline.

Triggers are now embedded in the fabric of his professional and personal life. Seeing a bicycle can leave him breathless. Being in crowded spaces, like the university quad between classes, feels intolerably dangerous. Most difficult, however, is being alone with women. This has made his work a minefield. During one-on-one meetings with his female graduate students, he is overcome with the conviction that he is in danger, that their benign professional manner is a mask. This perception immediately forces him into a state of rigid, forced composure. He focuses on controlling his emotions absolutely, believing any show of fear or anger would confirm his weakness. He has also stopped wearing his favourite flannel shirts, as his ex-wife was wearing one that day, and he avoids them as if the fabric itself were contaminated.

The strategies he uses to manage this constant sense of threat have only tightened the trap. His relentless effort to suppress all emotion seems to have further fractured the trauma memory; the more he pushes the feelings down, the more the event dissolves into those disconnected, terrifying snapshots. This, in turn, reinforces his belief that he is broken. The feeling of being constantly on guard has also cemented his negative appraisals; if the world requires this much vigilance, his conclusion that it is a treacherous place must be correct. His belief in his own inadequacy fuels his reliance on these rigid control strategies, creating a feedback loop of vigilance, suppression, and deepening despair. His professional identity has begun to crumble under the strain. He feels like a complete fraud, dispensing advice on healing while being fundamentally broken himself. It was this unbearable chasm between his public role and his private reality that finally made him agree with his wife: he could not fix this alone.
